source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Ko and Myers define a software error as the end of a chain of cognitive breakdowns, not a single slip. A breakdown is a failure in a programmer's skill, rule or knowledge-based activity (from Reason 1990). One breakdown can cause an error, the error causes a fault and a failure, the failure is misread, and that causes the next breakdown.
numbers: Framework has 3 breakdown classes (skill, rule, knowledge), 6 actions (create, reuse, modify, design, explore, understand) and 4 layers of defence in Fig 3 (specification, programmer, programming system, program).
quote: failures are ultimately due to a causal chain of failures both within and between layers of a system
limits: A descriptive taxonomy built from prior bug classifications plus Reason. It was not tested as a predictive model.
agent_relevance: Our agent can treat a wrong final answer as the end of a chain, not as one random mistake. The first wrong step is the one to find (G2), and the chain is what a trace must show.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Skill breakdowns are lapses of attention during routine actions: inattention (strong habit intrusion, interruption, delayed action, exceptional stimuli, interleaving) and overattention (omission, repetition after an attentional check). Rule breakdowns are wrong rule (problematic signs, information overload, favored rules, favored signs, rigidity) or bad rule (incomplete or inaccurate encoding, exception proves rule, wrong action).
numbers: Tables 3 and 4 list 5 inattention types, 2 overattention types, 5 wrong-rule types and 4 bad-rule types.
limits: Types are lifted from Reason, not derived from programming data. Authors say agreement was good on class but weaker on sub-type.
agent_relevance: Skill and rule slips map to LLM copy errors, off-by-one habits and pattern-matched wrong templates. These are the slips a code check catches, so G3 held-out tests are the right guard, not self-doubt (G1).

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Knowledge breakdowns come from bounded rationality and faulty models of the problem space. The named biases are selectivity, biased reviewing, availability, simplified causality, illusory correlation, overconfidence and confirmation bias. Debugging is where they bite: programmers form one or very few hypotheses and often pick a wrong one.
numbers: Table 5 lists 3 bounded-rationality types and 4 faulty-model types. Cites Gilmore (1991) and Vessey (1985) that debugging searches an unconstrained space and few hypotheses are considered.
limits: The knowledge class draws on general cognitive psychology; the mapping to specific programming biases is the authors' argument.
agent_relevance: This is the most agent-relevant part. A model that settles on one cause and edits there matches biased reviewing plus availability. Schema should force a second hypothesis only when a check fails (G1), and test each hypothesis against real output (G2).

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Method: think-aloud video of novice Alice programmers. Analysts find each runtime failure, trace back to the software errors, then to the breakdowns, and record each causal link with a timestamp. Two studies: Building Virtual Worlds (BVW, 3 undergraduates, own tasks, 50-245 min) and Pac-Man (4 HCI masters students, same task, 90-215 min).
numbers: 7 programmers, 895 minutes of video (about 15 h), about 40 h of analysis. BVW: B1 245, B2 110, B3 50 min. Pac-Man: P1 95, P2 90, P3 215, P4 90 min. One analyst coded all; a second coded a random 10% of failures; about 93% agreement on skill vs rule vs knowledge, lower on sub-type.
limits: Tiny sample (7), one system (Alice), novices, only errors that caused a visible runtime failure (silent errors were not counted), single main coder, percentages are over 159 breakdowns.
agent_relevance: Any claim from this paper is a hypothesis for LLM agents, not a measured fact. Use it to design traces we can code, and measure on LLMs ourselves.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Overall counts: 159 breakdowns, 69 of them roots (no earlier breakdown caused them), producing 102 software errors; 33 of those errors led to one or more new errors. Programmers spent 46.4% of their time debugging.
numbers: Table 9: total 895 min, 554 min debugging (46.4%), 102 errors, 159 breakdowns, 69 chains. Mean chain length 2.3 breakdowns (SD 2.2 in table; text says 2.3) and 1.5 errors per chain (SD 1.1). Per-person debugging share ranged from 22.0% (B3) to 76.7% (P3).
limits: Time share depends on task and Alice's poor runtime inspection. Chain length was longer for BVW (more complex code) than Pac-Man.
agent_relevance: About a third of errors spawned further errors. In an agent loop, a bad first patch is likely to seed follow-on bad patches, so rollback to a clean state (not patching on top) is worth testing.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Where breakdowns happened: 77.4% in implementation activity (skill 22.0%, rule 28.3%, knowledge 27.0%), 18.2% in runtime/debugging activity (skill 8.1%, rule 0.0%, knowledge 10.1%), 4.4% in specification (rule 3.1%, knowledge 1.2%, skill 0.0%). Roots were mostly knowledge breakdowns understanding failures and skill/rule breakdowns while coding.
numbers: Table 10, all percentages out of 159 breakdowns. Skill, rule and knowledge shares overall were about equal.
limits: Table 10 text extraction is garbled; the implementation, runtime and specification totals match the prose (77%, 18%) but the per-cell split should be checked against the PDF image.
agent_relevance: Roughly equal skill, rule and knowledge shares means no single guard covers the chain. We need a code check for slips and a hypothesis test for diagnosis.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Central result: the 18% of breakdowns made while forming hypotheses about runtime failures were behind nearly all the 24% of rule and skill breakdowns in modifying code. Typical path: programmer sees failure, forms a single wrong hypothesis (biased reviewing), has weak causal knowledge (simplified causality), edits the wrong code, and so adds a new error.
numbers: Debugging breakdowns 18% of total; modification breakdowns 24%; reuse breakdowns 7%. Author's text: only 18% of breakdowns caused nearly all of the errors introduced during fixing.
limits: Single system with almost no runtime data to test hypotheses (Alice), so the authors say the only test was to change the code. May overstate the effect in tools with good debuggers.
agent_relevance: This is the direct human analogue of an agent that edits from its own guess. It supports G2: a revision must cite real failing output. Debugging by editing is the failure path.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Example chain (P2, Pac-Man): wrong Boolean spec, wrong action, missing reference, biased reviewing (one hypothesis), wrong modification, problematic signs (camera moved so the failure was hidden), illusory correlation (believed it was fixed), and 20 minutes later availability (blamed recent edit instead of old wrong Boolean).
numbers: The bounce bug survived about 20 minutes unnoticed after the camera moved off it. Fig 8.
limits: One anecdote chain, no base rate for how often a chain looks like this.
agent_relevance: Shows how a non-visible failure was read as fixed. For the agent: a pass must not rest on the view we happened to look at (G3), and recent edits must not be blamed by default.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Most common cause of errors: rule breakdowns implementing complex Boolean expressions (33% of all breakdowns involved implementing Alice numerical and Boolean expressions). Example: 'if not (dot1.isEaten and dot2.isEaten)' is true if any dot is eaten. This confirms Pane's earlier finding that Boolean construction is error-prone.
numbers: 33% of all breakdowns; algorithms 37 breakdowns (23.3%), language constructs 35 (22.0%), animations/libraries 21 (13.2%), runtime failures 20 (12.6%), events 18 (11.3%), runtime faults 9 (5.7%), data structures 8 (5.0%). Software errors: algorithms 34 (33.3%), language 31 (30.4%), libraries 19 (18.6%).
limits: Alice-specific (visual language, off-screen operators). Negation slips are well known elsewhere too, but rates here are for novices.
agent_relevance: Negation and compound conditions are a concrete slip class to include in held-out checks (G3).

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: Reuse breakdowns (7% of all breakdowns) were rule breakdowns after copy and paste: programmers failed to adapt every reference to the new context, often because uncoerced references were off screen. These errors were hard to find because of overconfidence in copied code, and attention went to recent changes instead (availability).
numbers: 7% of breakdowns, and the longest debugging times in Table 12 were on rule breakdowns in reusing code and knowledge breakdowns in understanding code. Variance of debugging times was high.
limits: Small counts per cell (reuse errors 4 and 1 in Table 12 cells).
agent_relevance: Copy-adapt errors match LLMs reusing an example or earlier patch with stale names. Diff the reused text for leftover identifiers in code (G5: code selects).

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: The paper turns the breakdown data into ten design heuristics, including: help programmers consider all relevant hypotheses; help them find causal relationships; prevent overconfidence by testing assumptions; highlight logically important information. These were derived from the breakdown tables.
numbers: Table 13: 10 heuristics. Heuristics 6 and 10 map to hypothesis-set and assumption-testing.
limits: Heuristics are design advice, not tested individually in this paper.
agent_relevance: Heuristics 6, 7 and 10 read as a spec for a debugging operator: list alternative causes, test each assumption against output.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) A framework and methodology for studying the causes of software errors in programming systems
finding: The error chains inspired the Whyline. Right after a failure, programmers asked a why did or why didn't question that carried an unchecked assumption about runtime behavior. The Whyline lets them pick such a question and see the relevant runtime events, which removes the chance of forming a false hypothesis first.
numbers: Whyline reduced debugging time by a factor of about 8 and let programmers complete 40% more tasks (abstract of this paper, results from Ko and Myers 2004).
limits: Efficacy numbers come from a separate small CHI 2004 study (see a15, a16), not from the chain data.
agent_relevance: Design principle for the agent: convert the failure into an explicit question tied to observed output ('why did X not happen') before proposing any fix.

source: Ko and Myers (2003) Development and Evaluation of a Model of Programming Errors (IEEE HCC)
finding: Earlier version of the same model, labelled attentional, strategic and knowledge problems instead of skill, rule, knowledge. Same two Alice studies. Authors concluded most errors were attentional and strategic problems implementing algorithms, language constructs and library use, and that poor runtime inspection led to knowledge and attentional breakdowns about faults.
numbers: Same data: 895 min, 159 breakdowns, 102 errors, 69 chains. 29 knowledge and attentional breakdowns while determining faults and errors led to further errors. 24% of breakdowns were modification breakdowns. In Table 6 strategic problems caused 33 errors (32.4%) in implementing, modifying and reusing.
limits: Terminology changed between 2003 and 2005 (attentional/strategic vs skill/rule). Same 7 programmers, so not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Shows the label scheme was revised after the first pass; do not treat the category boundaries as fixed.

source: Ko and Myers (2003) Development and Evaluation of a Model of Programming Errors (IEEE HCC)
finding: Only quantitative links in the breakdown data: with 7 programmers, debugging time was strongly correlated with programming time, and number of errors with number of breakdowns.
numbers: Programming time vs debugging time r=.96, p<.001; programming time vs breakdowns r=.88, p<.01; errors vs breakdowns r=.95, p<.001; errors vs chains r=.90, p<.01; breakdowns vs debugging time r=.84, p<.05 (n=7 programmers).
limits: n=7, correlations mostly reflect session length (longer sessions have more of everything). No control for time.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Do not use these correlations as proof that breakdown count predicts cost.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions about Program Behavior (CHI)
finding: Formative studies behind the Whyline: about 50% of all errors were due to false assumptions in the hypotheses programmers formed while debugging existing errors. Questions programmers asked were mostly why didn't (68%), about code that plausibly could have run, and about a single object (85%).
numbers: 50% of errors tied to false hypotheses while debugging; 68% of questions were why didn't, 32% why did; 85% single-object.
limits: From Ko's two Alice studies, small samples, not independent of the 2005 paper. Programmers only asked why didn't about plausible code.
agent_relevance: The debugging question type we need to support is absence ('why did the output not change'), and agents need the trace to answer it, not a guess.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions about Program Behavior (CHI)
finding: Test of the tool: six identical debugging scenarios were compared between a With-Whyline study and a Without study. Time from failure to diagnosis fell by a factor of 7.8 on average. Example: 330 s without vs 38 s with, when the Whyline answered 'why didn't pac resize 0' with an invariant. In 90 minutes, Whyline users completed 3.20 tasks vs 2.25 without.
numbers: Repeated measures ANOVA on 6 scenarios: F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02. Tasks: with M=3.20 SD=.457, without M=2.25 SD=.500, t(7)=3.0, p<.02 (40% more). Participants found the Whyline useful for 19 of 24 questions, and usefulness rose from 0/3 (user E1) to 5/5 (E5).
limits: About 9 participants (5 with, 4 without), different people in each arm, 6 hand-picked matching scenarios, Alice only, authors' own tool, prototype changed between sessions. User E1 declared it useless when why-didn't was missing.
agent_relevance: Effect size is large but sample is tiny. It supports 'ask a causal question first', and we can run the LLM version cheaply to check.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented: Asking and Answering Why and Why Not Questions about Program Behavior (ICSE)
finding: Java Whyline pilot: 9 people (some had never seen code) debugged a slider bug with the Whyline. They finished in a median of 4 minutes (range 1-12) vs a median of 10 minutes (range 3-38) for 18 expert Java developers from an earlier study using Eclipse, p<.05. Experts asked the same question but first speculated about causes, then looked for a question that would check the guess.
numbers: Median 4 vs 10 min, Wilcoxon rank sums p<.05; whyline group more than twice as fast. Authors cite earlier work that developers' initial guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time.
quote: initial guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time
limits: Single task, 9 vs 18 participants, control group from a different earlier study with interruptions removed, novices vs experts confounded with tool. Authors say a preliminary unpublished expert-vs-expert result was 'twice as successful in half the time'.
agent_relevance: The expert habit of guessing first, then looking for a check, is the pattern our schema should block (G2): ask the question from observed output, not from a guessed cause.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Source-Level Debugging with the Whyline
finding: Controlled follow-up with 20 participants (10 per group) on two tasks adapted from real bug reports. All 10 Whyline users solved task one vs 3 of 10 controls; on task two 4 Whyline users succeeded vs none of the controls.
numbers: Task one 10/10 vs 3/10, chi2=10.6, p<.05; Whyline users twice as fast (t=4.5, p<0.05). Task two 4/10 vs 0/10 (chi2=5). Controls who finished 'got lucky' exploring hundreds of files vs a median of 3 files for Whyline users. 30 min limit.
limits: Two tasks, 20 people, tool built and tested by same group, short workshop-length paper.
agent_relevance: Second, larger test pointing the same way. The mechanism is replacing speculation with a question linked to observed output.

source: Ko, Myers and Aung (2004) Six Learning Barriers in End-User Programming Systems
finding: Same research group, different data: 40 non-programmers learning Visual Basic.NET, 130 sampled barriers across six types (design, selection, coordination, use, understanding, information). Understanding barriers (what the program did or why) were the largest and the hardest: 38 of 130, with 34 of 38 insurmountable. Invalid assumptions turned barriers insurmountable.
numbers: Understanding 38/130 with 34/38 insurmountable; design 4/130 with half insurmountable; selection 13/130. Barrier classification agreement 94%.
limits: Learners (not professionals), self-reported barriers, VB.NET only. A relative of the knowledge-breakdown idea but a separate dataset.
agent_relevance: Independent, larger source that failure to understand what the program actually did is the barrier that stops progress, supporting trace-first debugging.

source: Reason (1990) Human Error (Cambridge University Press)
finding: The source of the skill-rule-knowledge split (Rasmussen) and the Generic Error-Modelling System (GEMS): slips and lapses at the skill level, rule-based mistakes, knowledge-based mistakes, with 'latent errors' vs 'active errors'. Ko and Myers adapt its tables almost directly.
numbers: Not opened this session; description taken from how Ko and Myers (2005) use it.
limits: Book not read. Built on non-programming domains (industrial accidents). Ko and Myers carried it to programming without a test of whether the split is the best one for code.
agent_relevance: The error taxonomy is borrowed, not validated for LLMs. Treat skill/rule/knowledge as a labelling convenience.

source: Perkins and Martin (1986) Fragile knowledge and neglected strategies in novice programmers (as cited by Ko and Myers 2005)
finding: Cited by Ko and Myers: novice Pascal errors were mostly 'fragile knowledge' (knowledge that is present but not retrieved or applied). Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers recorded; secondhand via Ko and Myers 2005 section 2.3.2.
limits: Secondhand; original not read.
agent_relevance: Fragile knowledge resembles LLM answers that know a fact but fail to apply it unless cued; a held-out check (G3) would expose it.

source: Gilmore (1991) and Vessey (1985) on debugging hypotheses (as cited by Ko and Myers 2005)
finding: Cited by Ko and Myers: programmers consider only a few hypotheses and usually choose a wrong one, and debugging is hard because the range of causes is unconstrained and several faults can interact. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers recorded; secondhand.
limits: Secondhand. Original sample sizes unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a short list of alternative causes and testing each, but remember the base evidence here is old and human.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (ISSTA)
finding: From memory, not opened: a user study found that automated fault-localisation rankings did not clearly help programmers on harder bugs, which cautions that a better tool metric need not help people. Check before use.
numbers: Not recorded (not opened this session).
limits: Recalled from memory only; verify numbers and claims before citing.
agent_relevance: A caution to measure real task success, not tool metric gains.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR)
finding: Self-repair (model writes feedback on its own failing code, then repairs) is bottlenecked by the quality of the feedback, which is the diagnosis step in the breakdown chain. When the cost of repair samples is counted, repair often does no better than drawing fresh i.i.d. samples. Swapping in stronger-model or human feedback helps a lot.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each gave 1.05x the pass rate of pass@20; 2 samples with 10 repairs each gave 0.97x of pass@22. Human feedback raised repaired-and-passing fraction of programs from 33.3% to 52.6% (1.58x).
limits: Python only (HumanEval, APPS), models of 2023 (Code Llama-13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4), 16 human participants. Cost measured in tokens/samples.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: models locate errors poorly. Revise from real output, and put effort in the diagnosis step.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR)
finding: Human debuggers beat GPT-4's own explanations, especially on hard problems. GPT-4's feedback was wrong more often and never expressed uncertainty, while humans did.
numbers: Repair success with GPT-4 vs human feedback: introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%; overall 33.30% vs 52.60%. GPT-4 feedback judged obviously inaccurate in 32/80 vs 7/80 for humans; uncertainty expressed 0/80 vs 7/80. 16 participants (15 grad students, 1 professional), 80 human feedback strings.
limits: Small human sample; each program shown to two participants; time taken by humans not tracked.
agent_relevance: Models state wrong diagnoses with full confidence. A diagnosis from the model alone should not be accepted as an observation (G2, G4).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to review and correct its answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels, correction looks great, which explains earlier optimistic results.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 (standard) -> 75.1 (round 1) -> 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7, HotpotQA 29.0; GPT-4 97.5, 85.5, 59.0.
limits: Reasoning and QA tasks, not code. Main models are GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 of 2023. For GSM8K 74.7% of the time GPT-3.5 kept its answer; of the changes, more were correct-to-wrong.
agent_relevance: A model cannot tell the breakdown from its own text. G1 and G2: do not trigger revision from self-doubt; trigger it from a failing check.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: Evaluating Debugging Capability of Large Language Models (ACL Findings)
finding: Benchmark of 4,253 injected-bug LeetCode instances in C++, Java and Python across four bug classes (syntax, reference, logic, multiple) and 18 types. Models are good at surface slips and weak at logic and multiple errors. Humans (12 raters) still beat closed models.
numbers: GPT-4 pass rate: missing colons 93.6%, undefined objects 81.7%, operation error 68.6%, variable error 63.1%, triple bugs 58.9%, quadruple bugs 55.9%. GPT-3.5: missing colons 80.9%, operation error 49.5%, quadruple bugs 38.7%. Human results listed as x/12 (e.g. 8/12 on quadruple bugs).
limits: Bugs were implanted by GPT-4, judged realistic by raters but not from real commits. Pass rate on LeetCode tests. Models from 2023-24.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the human chain: surface (skill) slips are fixed, multi-cause bugs are not. Plan for tasks with more than one cause.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench
finding: Runtime feedback (tracebacks) helps for syntax and reference bugs but hurts or does not help for logic bugs in GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. Authors explain that tracebacks are too low level to point to the real logic cause.
numbers: Fig 4 effect of runtime feedback on gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0613: improves syntax and reference, impairs logic error resolution. Coding and debugging pass rates are strongly correlated for closed-source models.
limits: Effect shown in a figure; exact deltas not read from text. LeetCode single-function tasks.
agent_relevance: Raw traceback is not enough for logic faults. The scaffold should turn output into a targeted comparison (expected vs observed value) rather than just paste the trace (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (ICLR)
finding: Few-shot self-debugging with execution results and the model explaining its own code line by line ('rubber duck') improves code generation. Gains come mostly when real execution feedback is included.
numbers: MBPP accuracy (Codex / GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / StarCoder): baseline 61.4 / 67.6 / 72.8 / 47.2; with unit-test feedback 69.4 / 72.2 / 80.6 / 52.2; adding explanation 69.8 / 74.2 / 80.4 / 52.2; adding trace 70.8 / 72.8 / 80.2 / 53.2. Text: up to 12% on TransCoder, 2-3% on Spider with explanation only, 9% on hardest Spider level.
limits: Few-shot prompting, 2023 models, tasks with visible tests. Explanation alone (no execution) gives only 2-3%. Row labels of the MBPP table were read from garbled text; rows assumed in order Baseline, Simple, UT, +Expl, +Trace.
agent_relevance: Gains track real execution output, not reflection alone. Matches G2 and G3; also shows explanation adds little over unit-test results.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Debug like a Human: A Large Language Model Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step by Step (LDB)
finding: LDB splits a program into basic blocks, shows the model the intermediate variable values for each block, and asks it to judge each block correct or wrong. This follows how humans use a debugger and checks the chain of states, not only the final output.
numbers: Abstract: improves performance by up to 9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder with several backbones (GPT-3.5, CodeLlama, StarCoder).
limits: Python-style benchmarks with tests and seed programs from the same models. Improvement measured vs self-debug baselines of similar kind, not vs human debuggers. Per-cell table values were not cleanly readable.
agent_relevance: A trace-first operator exists and works on benchmarks. Use as a pattern for the agent's breakdown-location step.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching Large Language Models to Reason about Code Execution (ICML)
finding: Training a model to write chain-of-thought rationales grounded in line-by-line execution traces (variable states) improves program repair.
numbers: PaLM 2 fix rate improved by 26.1% absolute on MBPP-R and 14.3% absolute on HumanEval-R; rationale quality checked by automated metrics and human raters; also generalised to settings without traces.
limits: Needs fine-tuning (self-training); not a prompting-only result. Repair sets are derived from MBPP/HumanEval.
agent_relevance: Same lesson without training: give the agent an observed trace. Our scaffold cannot fine-tune, but can supply traces from code.

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) Improved Bug Localization with AI Agents Leveraging Hypothesis and Dynamic Cognition (ICPC 2026)
finding: CogniGent: multi-agent bug localisation that mimics human debugging (hypotheses on root cause, call-graph traversal, hypothesis testing, observer agent). Beats six baselines on 591 bug reports. Removing hypothesis testing costs the most.
numbers: MAP improvements of 23.33-38.57% (document and method level), MRR improvements of 25.14-53.74%. Ablation: removing the investigation module lowers method-level MAP to 0.183, a 19.02% drop; hypothesis generation and testing drive the largest gains (up to 19%).
limits: Bug localisation (finding the file or method), not repair. Dataset extended from Bench4BL; baselines include Agentless and LocAgent.
agent_relevance: A 2026 positive result for explicit hypothesis then test, the very step Ko and Myers say humans skip. Fits an operator that must test a hypothesis against evidence.

source: Majgaonkar et al. (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: An Empirical Study of Success and Failure Trajectories
finding: Failed agent trajectories on SWE-Bench are longer and more varied than successful ones. Agents usually find the right file, so failure is in fine-grained reasoning, not navigation. They spend as long on wrong paths as on right ones and do not abandon them.
numbers: Failed trajectories longer by 12.6% (SWE-agent, Lite) and 18.5% (Verified); OpenHands 31.0% and 82.5%. 72-81% of trajectories located the problematic file even when failing; successful patches hit the right file over 90% of the time.
limits: Three agents (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus), SWE-Bench Lite and Verified; correlational. Step counts depend on agent verbosity.
agent_relevance: The 'slip' is rarely a wrong file; it is a wrong local belief. Add a loop detector and abandon rule from code, not self-judgment (G1).

source: Mehta (2026) Confident and Wrong: Silent Semantic Failures in Coding Agents
finding: Most failures of coding agents are 'silent semantic failures': the agent submits a plausible patch on every run but none pass, repeating the same misinterpretation of the bug rather than random errors. Pre-edit prompts that ask the agent to state its understanding did not help.
numbers: 1,750 trajectories on 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 4 models. GPT-5 submits 100% but resolves 44%; Llama 4 submits 99%, resolves 18%; Gemini submits 70%, resolves 50%. Silent semantic failure covers 80% (Llama 4) and 68% (GPT-5) of failing runs. Interpretation guard: Claude 65.2% to 64.8%, GPT-5 44.4% to 46.0%.
limits: Single study, 50 tasks, 5 runs each, models of 2025-26. Silent failure defined as 5/5 submit and 0/5 resolve, so it needs repeated runs to measure.
agent_relevance: Directly supports G4: repeated agreement is not correctness, because the same wrong reading is re-derived. Only held-out tests (G3) separate them.

source: Mehta (2026) Confident and Wrong: Silent Semantic Failures in Coding Agents
finding: Action bias: when the bug is already fixed (gold patch pre-applied), models still edit correct code instead of stopping.
numbers: On 60-90% of runs (n=50 per model) every model edited correct code; only GPT-5 abstained cleanly with any frequency (40%). Best-of-3 raises Claude 65 to 74% and GPT-5 44 to 58% (per paper). A 3-gram loop detector caught 100% of Gemini's no-submit tasks with no false positives.
limits: Probe on a subset of tasks; bug report left unchanged so a 'fix' is a reasonable reading of the prompt. Models 2025-26.
agent_relevance: The agent needs a check that can say 'no defect found'. Add an abstain outcome in S-states, and make passing tests before editing a stop signal.

source: Qi et al. (2026) TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
finding: Agent failures look like Ko and Myers' chains: one critical (earliest decisive) error, many other local errors. Most local errors are repaired later; some persist. Locating the critical step from the failed trajectory alone is hard for LLMs and gets worse with length.
numbers: From 50 annotated failed trajectories: 381 local errors, 7.62 per trajectory, one critical each. Of 331 non-critical, 205 (61.9%) were later repaired, 104 (31.4%) persisted, 22 (6.6%) dormant. TRAJERRBENCH: 486 trajectories. TRAJDEBUG macro accuracy 34.11% vs 25.69% direct prompting (+8.42). Injecting its diagnosis as guidance improved success by 10.80% on average.
limits: Absolute accuracy for finding the critical step is low (34%). Benchmark built by the authors with 3 annotators; includes tau2-Bench and SWE-Bench Pro.
agent_relevance: The most direct 2026 analogue of the chain-from-slip-to-defect method for LLMs. It also shows LLM judges cannot reliably find the root step, so G2 says use code to locate it.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) framework: limits of evidence base
finding: No independent replication or failed replication of the Alice breakdown percentages was found in this session. The numbers rest on 7 novices in one system. Later work by the same author (Whyline CHI 2004, ICSE 2008, 2008 short paper) tests the debugging-cause claim indirectly through a tool, not the breakdown percentages.
numbers: Counts: 7 programmers, 159 breakdowns, 69 root breakdowns. WebSearch was cut off by the session budget; arXiv-only search for LLM follow-ups was done. Absence of a replication here is 'not found', not 'does not exist'.
limits: Search coverage of human-factors literature (Ko 2006+ field studies, Parnin and Orso, Beller et al.) was limited; other angles should check them.
agent_relevance: Treat the breakdown percentages as one weak data point; rely on the LLM trajectory studies for numbers that apply to agents.
